content_html:
Building internal observability for AI coding agents? Start here.

Open-source collectors for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Windsurf, plus an editor extension for VS Code and Cursor. They capture what your agents do as structured events, without prompts, responses or source code. Run them locally, send the events to your own tools, or fork the project and build your own engineering analytics. Skip building and maintaining the collection layer, and spend the time on what you measure. No Ascenda account needed.

$ node examples/local-event-reader/read-events.mjs --follow
Watching ~/.ascenda/events.jsonl. Ctrl-C to stop.
07:29:39 AM  Claude Code  session.started
07:29:41 AM  Claude Code  prompt.submitted
07:29:44 AM  Claude Code  tool.started Read
07:29:45 AM  Claude Code  tool.completed Read
07:29:47 AM  Codex        prompt.submitted
07:29:49 AM  Claude Code  tool.started Edit
07:29:50 AM  Claude Code  tool.completed Edit
07:29:52 AM  Codex        tool.started local_shell
07:29:53 AM  Claude Code  tool.started Bash
07:29:56 AM  Codex        tool.failed local_shell (failure)
07:29:58 AM  Claude Code  tool.failed Bash (failure)
07:30:00 AM  Claude Code  agent.waiting
07:30:02 AM  Claude Code  turn.completed

A Claude Code session and a Codex session side by side, read by a small script with no dependencies. The hook payloads were replayed through the real collectors, so you can run the same thing. Install any agent's hooks with --no-pair and you get this file.

Why these collectors

Every coding agent reports its work differently. Different hooks, different event formats, different ideas of what a session is, and each changes every few weeks. Keeping a collection layer working across all of them is a project of its own, and collecting conversations brings security and governance problems you don't want.

  • Activity, not conversations. Structured events. Never prompt or response text, file contents or command output.
  • One format across agents. Every agent's events map to the same small schema, agent-event/v0.
  • Local first. Installed without pairing, the hooks write events to a file on the machine. Nothing leaves it.
  • Yours to build on. Feed your own dashboards, internal tools or research. Collecting from a team gets every engineer's events into one place.
  • Open source. Apache-2.0. Fork it, extend it, and send improvements back.

What these events do and don't tell you is set out in What this measures.

See how you work with your agents Ascenda Flow, free for individual engineers

Waterline is the quickest way to see the collectors working: a free macOS screen saver that turns Claude Code, Codex and Cursor activity into a water level. It runs on your Mac, with no account. See Waterline

Install

Pick the tools you use. Each works alone, and each has its own pairing.

Agent Command Hooks registered in
Claude Code npx -y @ascenda-one/claude-code-hooks setup ~/.claude/settings.json
Codex CLI npx -y @ascenda-one/codex-hooks setup ~/.codex/hooks.json
Cursor (agent) npx -y @ascenda-one/cursor-hooks setup ~/.cursor/hooks.json
Windsurf npx -y @ascenda-one/windsurf-hooks setup ~/.codeium/windsurf/hooks.json
Gemini CLI npx -y @ascenda-one/gemini-hooks setup ~/.gemini/settings.json

If you've set CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or CODEX_HOME, setup writes there.

Add --no-pair to install without an account. setup then installs the hooks and stops. The live signal and the local event log work, and nothing is sent.

What setup does, for every agent:

  • Registers the hooks for every project. --scope project limits them to the current folder instead. Re-running setup moves an older install from the other place, so each event runs once.
  • Installs a launcher that finds Node. Each hook runs ~/.ascenda/bin/ascenda-<agent>-hook, a small shell script that uses the Node 20+ that ran setup and finds another if that one goes (Homebrew, nvm, fnm, volta, asdf, mise). Hooks keep working when the agent starts from the Dock or an IDE without your shell's PATH. On Windows the hook runs the Node that ran setup directly.
  • Pairs, unless you passed --no-pair: it prints a 6-digit code to confirm in the Flow app under Connections → Ingest telemetry.

Nothing goes in your shell profile. Then restart the agent:

  • Claude Code: type /hooks. The Ascenda hooks are listed under User.
  • Codex: open /hooks and trust the Ascenda hooks. Codex doesn't run a hook until you do.

Check it works

~/.ascenda/bin/ascenda-claude-hook doctor     # or ascenda-codex-hook, -cursor-, -gemini-, -windsurf-

doctor checks the local half first, which needs no pairing. Can the hooks start, are they registered where the agent loads them, has the agent run one yet, and is anything listening for the live signal. When the screen saver is running it pings it and waits for the answer. Every line says how to fix what it finds.

status is the short version, and exits non-zero when something is missing, so it can gate a CI step. uninstall removes the hooks, the launcher and the pairing.

Claude Code: the plugin, or setup

The Claude Code plugin installs the hooks together with the work-signals skill and the MCP server:

claude plugin marketplace add ascendaone-com/ai-engineer-tools
claude plugin install ascenda@ascenda-one

Its hooks run through npx, so they need Node on the PATH Claude Code was started with, and they don't get the launcher. Use the plugin or setup for the hooks, not both: with both, every event runs twice.

VS Code and the Cursor editor

The editor extension records editor and terminal activity. It is one extension for both editors.

  1. Open the Extensions pane (⇧⌘X, or Ctrl+Shift+X on Windows and Linux).

  2. Search Ascenda and click Install. The publisher is ascenda-one.

  3. Open the Command Palette (⇧⌘P / Ctrl+Shift+P) and run Ascenda: Connect App.

From the command line instead:

code   --install-extension ascenda-one.ascenda   # VS Code
cursor --install-extension ascenda-one.ascenda   # Cursor

On macOS those commands aren't on PATH until you run Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH from the Command Palette.

The event format

Install any agent's hooks with --no-pair and every event lands in ~/.ascenda/events.jsonl. Each line's event field follows an open, versioned format: which agent, what happened, which tool, how it ended. It's documented in packages/agent-events, and examples/local-event-reader is a dependency-free script that reads it. Build a dashboard, feed your own tool, or check what the collectors record. None of it needs an Ascenda account.

The format is v0 and experimental. If you build on it, tell us what's missing in an issue: that's what decides v1.

What each agent can report

The agents expose different hooks, so they can't all say the same things. A gap here is the agent's hook set, not something we infer around.

Claude Code Codex Cursor Gemini CLI Windsurf
Working (prompts, tool calls) yes yes yes yes yes
Waiting on you (an approval) yes yes no hook yes no hook
Context compaction yes yes yes yes no hook
Quit mid-turn ends the session yes no hook yes yes no hook

Each package's README lists its events in full.

Privacy and the local-first design

The collectors work in two ways, and the first needs no account:

  • On your machine only. The hooks write every event to ~/.ascenda/events.jsonl and send a live signal to a socket on your Mac, which Waterline and the Flow app read. Nothing leaves the machine.
  • With your Ascenda account. Pair a tool once and its events go to Ascenda, so your sessions appear in Flow over time. The live signal keeps working, and setup --event-log keeps the local file as well.

Workspace identifiers are hashed with a random salt generated on first run and stored only at ~/.ascenda/salt. It is never sent, so the hashes can't be turned back into folder or repository names by anyone holding the telemetry. Deleting the file resets the hashes.

Metadata only, by default. Not a medical device: it measures workload patterns for self-awareness, not diagnosis or treatment, and makes no clinical claim. Consent is scoped and separately revocable: ide_telemetry for editor and agent signals, workflow_telemetry for collaboration signals, and semantic_work_signals for the patterns an agent reports. Granting one does not grant the others.

What the metadata-only guarantee covers on each surface is listed in each package's README under Privacy defaults, including where it is enforced by schema rather than convention: the semantic signal tool rejects free text outright.

Building something with these collectors?

We'd like to hear what you're measuring. Tell us in an issue if you're building internal analytics on these events, extending the collectors, or working out how your team uses agents.

  • Read the events. packages/agent-events has the schema, the types and a reader. examples/local-event-reader is a working starting point, and Collecting from a team covers getting everyone's events into one place.
  • Add an agent. Each collector is a thin adapter over a shared runtime. CONTRIBUTING.md walks through adding one, and how to test it with no backend.
  • Report what breaks. Agents change their hooks often. The issue forms take a compatibility report or a proposal for a new integration.

If you'd rather compare notes with other teams, the Founding Benchmark is bringing 200 AI-native teams together to do that.

Forks and commercial products built on these collectors are welcome under Apache-2.0.

Pairing

Pairing links one tool installation to your Ascenda account. Each tool pairs on its own, and each pairing can be revoked on its own in the Flow app.

The editor extension pairs with Ascenda: Connect App, which shows a QR code and a six-digit code, good for a few minutes:

Confirm it in the Flow app under Connections → Ingest telemetry: scan the QR, or paste the code. The code carries no personal data.

The CLI agents pair during setup, which prints the same kind of code. To pair an install made with --no-pair, run setup again (or, for Claude Code, ~/.ascenda/bin/ascenda-claude-hook pair). It attaches to the installation already on file, so the hooks you have keep their identity.

The editor's pairing can't be shared with the CLI agents: its token lives in the editor's own secret storage, by design. Each CLI agent keeps its pairing under its own key in ~/.ascenda/credentials.json, so several agents on one machine never borrow each other's identity. ASCENDA_TOOL_INSTALLATION_ID overrides that for every agent at once; set it only if you mean that.

A setup whose pairing can't finish (the server unreachable, the code not confirmed in time) still installs the hooks, and says plainly that it isn't paired.

Upgrading

An install keeps the hooks it registered until setup runs again, so a release that adds a hook reaches you on the next setup. The Flow app says so in Connections → Ingest telemetry and names the command.

npx -y @ascenda-one/claude-code-hooks setup     # or codex-, cursor-, gemini-, windsurf-hooks

setup is safe to re-run. It keeps your pairing, replaces its own entries, and prints what it added. Restart the agent afterwards. A plugin install upgrades with claude plugin update ascenda@ascenda-one instead.

Packages

Package Published as What it does
ascenda-claude-code-hooks @ascenda-one/claude-code-hooks (npm) Claude Code hooks: prompts, tool calls, compaction, waits, subagents
ascenda-codex-hooks @ascenda-one/codex-hooks (npm) Codex CLI hooks, through Codex's hooks.json
ascenda-cursor-hooks @ascenda-one/cursor-hooks (npm) Cursor agent hooks
ascenda-windsurf-hooks @ascenda-one/windsurf-hooks (npm) Windsurf Cascade hooks; the gaps in Windsurf's hook set are documented, not filled in
ascenda-gemini-hooks @ascenda-one/gemini-hooks (npm) Gemini CLI hooks; the per-inference hooks are deliberately left unregistered
ascenda-vscode-extension-telemetry ascenda-one.ascenda (VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX) The editor extension for VS Code and Cursor: editor activity, terminal classification, sessions
ascenda-agent-skills ascenda@ascenda-one (Claude Code plugin) The plugin: the work-signals skill, the hooks and the MCP server in one install, plus the Cursor rule
ascenda-agent-mcp @ascenda-one/agent-mcp (npm) MCP server exposing ascenda_emit_work_signal, for patterns only the agent can see
ascenda-history-import @ascenda-one/history-import (npm) Reads the AI-tool history already on your machine (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, git) into a baseline
ascenda-github-collector @ascenda-one/github-collector (npm) Your own review load and pull request activity from a code forge, never anyone else's
ascenda-pairing-sim not published Stands in for the app in pairing tests: confirm, list, revoke, end to end
ascenda-dev-server not published A local mock of the /v1 pairing and ingest API, so any tool runs with no backend. Binds to 127.0.0.1

Shared packages

The repo is an npm workspace. The tools above are thin shells over these:

Package Role
packages/tool-contract The event catalog, DTOs and constants, declared once. Mirrors the Tool Pairing API Reference
packages/tool-kit The shared runtime: setup, status and doctor for the CLI agents, the hook launcher, the live signal, the command classifier, the token store and the /v1 client
packages/ide-extension-core The single extension implementation; whether it runs in VS Code or Cursor is detected at runtime
packages/agent-events @ascenda-one/agent-events on npm. The public event format, v0 and experimental: a JSON Schema, types and a log reader

Build from source

You don't need this to use the tools. It's here because "verify what you're running" is a reasonable thing to want from a telemetry tool, and the repo is Apache-2.0 so you can.

npm install
npm run build     # shared packages first, then the tools
npm run verify    # the DRY guard rail (scripts/check-dry.sh), a full build, and every test

The extension is bundled with esbuild at package time (npm run package), so the shared packages are inlined. Each package's README has its own development notes.

Install from a release (no registry)

For machines that can't reach the Marketplace or npm, or for anyone who wants to check a checksum first. Every tagged release attaches each artifact and a manifest.json; resolve downloads through the manifest rather than from main. Requires Node 20+.

BASE=https://github.com/ascendaone-com/ai-engineer-tools/releases/latest/download
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/manifest.json"
cat manifest.json    # { version, minNode, artifacts: [{ name, url, sha256 }] }

The editor extension. One VSIX for both editors:

curl -fsSLO "$BASE/ascenda-<version>.vsix"
code   --install-extension ./ascenda-<version>.vsix   # VS Code
cursor --install-extension ./ascenda-<version>.vsix   # Cursor

Prefer the Marketplace or Open VSX when you can reach them; you get updates.

The hooks. Each is a self-contained ESM file with no dependencies. Download it anywhere and run its setup, which installs the launcher and the bundle in ~/.ascenda/bin. No sudo, no npm -g, nothing to add to PATH:

curl -fsSLO "$BASE/ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs"
node ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs setup --no-pair

Verify before you run. Check the checksum against the manifest, and optionally the build provenance:

shasum -a 256 ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs        # must match sha256 in manifest.json
gh attestation verify ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs --repo ascendaone-com/ai-engineer-tools

Releases are built only by .github/workflows/release.yml, gated on npm run verify, and signed with keyless Sigstore build provenance.

Developing on this repo

TESTING.md runs everything with no backend, phone or sign-in: ./scripts/dev-quickstart.sh gets events flowing against ascenda-dev-server in about two minutes.

To pair against a dev backend without a phone:

ascenda-pairing-sim e2e --tool-type cursor_mcp

Point a CLI at another backend with ASCENDA_API_BASE_URL, or the extension with the ascenda.apiBaseUrl setting. Never commit tokens.

The terminal screenshots above are rendered from the real CLI by node scripts/render-cli-shots.mjs; re-run it when the output changes. See docs/images.

What this measures

What it records. Events you can name: prompts and corrections, tool calls and how they ended, test and build runs, context compaction, how long agent loops run, how many agents are going at once, and work outside your usual hours. Counts and classifications, set against your own history.

What we're testing. Whether patterns like these shift before you notice the work getting heavier, and whether your own baseline shows that sooner than you'd see it yourself. That's the question the collectors were built to answer. We don't have the answer yet.

What's still open. No published study yet links agent activity like this to a validated measure of workload, and our own calibration study hasn't run. Today the collectors count what happened and show it against your history. The source is here, so you can check exactly what that means.

content_html_zh:
Building internal observability for AI coding agents? 从这里开始。

Open-source collectors for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Windsurf, plus an editor extension for VS Code and Cursor. They capture what your agents do as structured events, without prompts, responses or source code. Run them locally, send the events to your own tools, or fork the project and build your own engineering analytics. Skip building and maintaining the collection layer, and spend the time on what you measure. No Ascenda account needed.

$ node examples/local-event-reader/read-events.mjs --follow
Watching ~/.ascenda/events.jsonl. Ctrl-C to stop.
07:29:39 AM  Claude Code  session.started
07:29:41 AM  Claude Code  prompt.submitted
07:29:44 AM  Claude Code  tool.started Read
07:29:45 AM  Claude Code  tool.completed Read
07:29:47 AM  Codex        prompt.submitted
07:29:49 AM  Claude Code  tool.started Edit
07:29:50 AM  Claude Code  tool.completed Edit
07:29:52 AM  Codex        tool.started local_shell
07:29:53 AM  Claude Code  tool.started Bash
07:29:56 AM  Codex        tool.failed local_shell (failure)
07:29:58 AM  Claude Code  tool.failed Bash (failure)
07:30:00 AM  Claude Code  agent.waiting
07:30:02 AM  Claude Code  turn.completed

A Claude Code session and a Codex session side by side, read by a small script with no dependencies. The hook payloads were replayed through the real collectors, so you can run the same thing. Install any agent's hooks with --no-pair and you get this file.

Why these collectors

Every coding agent reports its work differently. Different hooks, different event formats, different ideas of what a session is, and each changes every few weeks. Keeping a collection layer working across all of them is a project of its own, and collecting conversations brings security and governance problems you don't want.

  • Activity, not conversations. Structured events. Never prompt or response text, file contents or command output.
  • One format across agents. Every agent's events map to the same small schema, agent-event/v0.
  • 本地优先。 Installed without pairing, the hooks write events to a file on the machine. Nothing leaves it.
  • Yours to build on. Feed your own dashboards, internal tools or research. Collecting from a team gets every engineer's events into one place.
  • 开源。 阿帕奇-2.0。 Fork it, extend it, and send improvements back.

What these events do and don't tell you is set out in What this measures.

三种使用方法

You want to Start with
Build your own analytics across the team The collectors, then Collecting from a team
See how you work with your agents Ascenda Flow, free for individual engineers
Compare your team with other AI-native teams The Founding Benchmark

Counts tell you what happened. Whether a busy week was a good one, whether a change helped, and how you compare with other teams takes each person's own read of their days, and other teams to compare with. That's what Flow and the benchmark add.

Waterline is the quickest way to see the collectors working: a free macOS screen saver that turns Claude Code, Codex and Cursor activity into a water level. It runs on your Mac, with no account. See Waterline

Waterline with Ascenda Flow paired, at double speed. Flow gives the water its colour.

Ascenda Flow is a macOS app that shows how you work with your agents: how many you run at once, when your best work happens, and what gets in the way. It starts from the history Claude Code, Cursor and Codex already keep on your Mac. Free for individual engineers, with invitations going out by email. 抢先体验

Flow's HUD while agents work, about 8× speed.

The Founding Benchmark studies how small AI-native teams work with agents: concurrency, who carries the review load, steering and rework. We're inviting 200 teams of roughly 2 to 15 engineers, selected in waves of 20. Selected teams get early access to Flow, and a comparison with similar teams once the cohort has enough of them. It's free, and each engineer decides whether to take part. Apply with your team

安装

Pick the tools you use. Each works alone, and each has its own pairing.

Agent 命令 Hooks registered in
克劳德·科德 npx -y @ascenda-one/claude-code-hooks setup 〜/.claude/settings.json
法典 CLI npx -y @ascenda-one/codex-hooks setup 〜/.codex/hooks.json
Cursor (agent) npx -y @ascenda-one/cursor-hooks setup 〜/.cursor/hooks.json
风帆冲浪 npx -y @ascenda-one/windsurf-hooks setup 〜/.codeium/windsurf/hooks.json
双子座命令行界面 npx -y @ascenda-one/gemini-hooks setup 〜/.gemini/settings.json

If you've set CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or CODEX_HOME, setup writes there.

Add --no-pair to install without an account. setup then installs the hooks and stops. The live signal and the local event log work, and nothing is sent.

What setup does, for every agent:

  • Registers the hooks for every project. --scope project limits them to the current folder instead. Re-running setup moves an older install from the other place, so each event runs once.
  • Installs a launcher that finds Node. Each hook runs ~/.ascenda/bin/ascenda-<agent>-hook, a small shell script that uses the Node 20+ that ran setup and finds another if that one goes (Homebrew, nvm, fnm, volta, asdf, mise). Hooks keep working when the agent starts from the Dock or an IDE without your shell's PATH. On Windows the hook runs the Node that ran setup directly.
  • Pairs, unless you passed --no-pair: it prints a 6-digit code to confirm in the Flow app under Connections → Ingest telemetry.

Nothing goes in your shell profile. Then restart the agent:

  • Claude Code: type /hooks. The Ascenda hooks are listed under User.
  • Codex: open /hooks and trust the Ascenda hooks. Codex doesn't run a hook until you do.

检查是否有效

~/.ascenda/bin/ascenda-claude-hook doctor     # or ascenda-codex-hook, -cursor-, -gemini-, -windsurf-

doctor checks the local half first, which needs no pairing. Can the hooks start, are they registered where the agent loads them, has the agent run one yet, and is anything listening for the live signal. When the screen saver is running it pings it and waits for the answer. Every line says how to fix what it finds.

status is the short version, and exits non-zero when something is missing, so it can gate a CI step. uninstall removes the hooks, the launcher and the pairing.

Claude Code: the plugin, or setup

The Claude Code plugin installs the hooks together with the work-signals skill and the MCP server:

claude plugin marketplace add ascendaone-com/ai-engineer-tools
claude plugin install ascenda@ascenda-one

Its hooks run through npx, so they need Node on the PATH Claude Code was started with, and they don't get the launcher. Use the plugin or setup for the hooks, not both: with both, every event runs twice.

VS Code and the Cursor editor

The editor extension records editor and terminal activity. It is one extension for both editors.

  1. Open the Extensions pane (⇧⌘X, or Ctrl+Shift+X on Windows and Linux).
  2. Search Ascenda and click Install. The publisher is ascenda-one.
  3. Open the Command Palette (⇧⌘P / Ctrl+Shift+P) and run Ascenda: Connect App.

From the command line instead:

code   --install-extension ascenda-one.ascenda   # VS Code
cursor --install-extension ascenda-one.ascenda   # Cursor

On macOS those commands aren't on PATH until you run Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH from the Command Palette.

The event format

Install any agent's hooks with --no-pair and every event lands in ~/.ascenda/events.jsonl. Each line's event field follows an open, versioned format: which agent, what happened, which tool, how it ended. It's documented in packages/agent-events, and examples/local-event-reader is a dependency-free script that reads it. Build a dashboard, feed your own tool, or check what the collectors record. None of it needs an Ascenda account.

The format is v0 and experimental. If you build on it, tell us what's missing in an issue: that's what decides v1.

What each agent can report

The agents expose different hooks, so they can't all say the same things. A gap here is the agent's hook set, not something we infer around.

克劳德·科德 Codex 光标 双子座命令行界面 风帆冲浪
Working (prompts, tool calls) yes yes yes yes yes
Waiting on you (an approval) yes yes no hook yes no hook
Context compaction yes yes yes yes no hook
Quit mid-turn ends the session yes no hook yes yes no hook

Each package's README lists its events in full.

Privacy and the local-first design

The collectors work in two ways, and the first needs no account:

  • On your machine only. The hooks write every event to ~/.ascenda/events.jsonl and send a live signal to a socket on your Mac, which Waterline and the Flow app read. Nothing leaves the machine.
  • With your Ascenda account. Pair a tool once and its events go to Ascenda, so your sessions appear in Flow over time. The live signal keeps working, and setup --event-log keeps the local file as well.

Workspace identifiers are hashed with a random salt generated on first run and stored only at ~/.ascenda/salt. It is never sent, so the hashes can't be turned back into folder or repository names by anyone holding the telemetry. Deleting the file resets the hashes.

Metadata only, by default. Not a medical device: it measures workload patterns for self-awareness, not diagnosis or treatment, and makes no clinical claim. Consent is scoped and separately revocable: ide_telemetry for editor and agent signals, workflow_telemetry for collaboration signals, and semantic_work_signals for the patterns an agent reports. Granting one does not grant the others.

What the metadata-only guarantee covers on each surface is listed in each package's README under Privacy defaults, including where it is enforced by schema rather than convention: the semantic signal tool rejects free text outright.

Building something with these collectors?

We'd like to hear what you're measuring. Tell us in an issue if you're building internal analytics on these events, extending the collectors, or working out how your team uses agents.

  • Read the events. packages/agent-events has the schema, the types and a reader. examples/local-event-reader is a working starting point, and Collecting from a team covers getting everyone's events into one place.
  • Add an agent. Each collector is a thin adapter over a shared runtime. CONTRIBUTING.md walks through adding one, and how to test it with no backend.
  • Report what breaks. Agents change their hooks often. The issue forms take a compatibility report or a proposal for a new integration.

If you'd rather compare notes with other teams, the Founding Benchmark is bringing 200 AI-native teams together to do that.

Forks and commercial products built on these collectors are welcome under Apache-2.0.

Pairing

Pairing links one tool installation to your Ascenda account. Each tool pairs on its own, and each pairing can be revoked on its own in the Flow app.

The editor extension pairs with Ascenda: Connect App, which shows a QR code and a six-digit code, good for a few minutes:

Confirm it in the Flow app under Connections → Ingest telemetry: scan the QR, or paste the code. The code carries no personal data.

The CLI agents pair during setup, which prints the same kind of code. To pair an install made with --no-pair, run setup again (or, for Claude Code, ~/.ascenda/bin/ascenda-claude-hook pair). It attaches to the installation already on file, so the hooks you have keep their identity.

The editor's pairing can't be shared with the CLI agents: its token lives in the editor's own secret storage, by design. Each CLI agent keeps its pairing under its own key in ~/.ascenda/credentials.json, so several agents on one machine never borrow each other's identity. ASCENDA_TOOL_INSTALLATION_ID overrides that for every agent at once; set it only if you mean that.

A setup whose pairing can't finish (the server unreachable, the code not confirmed in time) still installs the hooks, and says plainly that it isn't paired.

升级中

npx -y @ascenda-one/claude-code-hooks setup     # or codex-, cursor-, gemini-, windsurf-hooks

setup is safe to re-run. It keeps your pairing, replaces its own entries, and prints what it added. Restart the agent afterwards. A plugin install upgrades with claude plugin update ascenda@ascenda-one instead.

从源代码构建

You don't need this to use the tools. It's here because "verify what you're running" is a reasonable thing to want from a telemetry tool, and the repo is Apache-2.0 so you can.

npm install
npm run build     # shared packages first, then the tools
npm run verify    # the DRY guard rail (scripts/check-dry.sh), a full build, and every test

The extension is bundled with esbuild at package time (npm run package), so the shared packages are inlined. Each package's README has its own development notes.

Install from a release (no registry)

For machines that can't reach the Marketplace or npm, or for anyone who wants to check a checksum first. Every tagged release attaches each artifact and a manifest.json; resolve downloads through the manifest rather than from main. 需要节点 20+。

BASE=https://github.com/ascendaone-com/ai-engineer-tools/releases/latest/download
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/manifest.json"
cat manifest.json    # { version, minNode, artifacts: [{ name, url, sha256 }] }

The editor extension. One VSIX for both editors:

curl -fsSLO "$BASE/ascenda-<version>.vsix"
code   --install-extension ./ascenda-<version>.vsix   # VS Code
cursor --install-extension ./ascenda-<version>.vsix   # Cursor

Prefer the Marketplace or Open VSX when you can reach them; you get updates.

The hooks. Each is a self-contained ESM file with no dependencies. Download it anywhere and run its setup, which installs the launcher and the bundle in ~/.ascenda/bin. No sudo, no npm -g, nothing to add to PATH:

curl -fsSLO "$BASE/ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs"
node ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs setup --no-pair

Verify before you run. Check the checksum against the manifest, and optionally the build provenance:

shasum -a 256 ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs        # must match sha256 in manifest.json
gh attestation verify ascenda-codex-hooks.mjs --repo ascendaone-com/ai-engineer-tools

Releases are built only by .github/workflows/release.yml, gated on npm run verify, and signed with keyless Sigstore build provenance.

Developing on this repo

TESTING.md runs everything with no backend, phone or sign-in: ./scripts/dev-quickstart.sh gets events flowing against ascenda-dev-server in about two minutes.

To pair against a dev backend without a phone:

ascenda-pairing-sim e2e --tool-type cursor_mcp

Point a CLI at another backend with ASCENDA_API_BASE_URL, or the extension with the ascenda.apiBaseUrl setting. Never commit tokens.

What this measures

What it records. Events you can name: prompts and corrections, tool calls and how they ended, test and build runs, context compaction, how long agent loops run, how many agents are going at once, and work outside your usual hours. Counts and classifications, set against your own history.

What we're testing. Whether patterns like these shift before you notice the work getting heavier, and whether your own baseline shows that sooner than you'd see it yourself. That's the question the collectors were built to answer. We don't have the answer yet.

What's still open. No published study yet links agent activity like this to a validated measure of workload, and our own calibration study hasn't run. Today the collectors count what happened and show it against your history. The source is here, so you can check exactly what that means.
